'''Pierre Frédéric Sarrus''' ({{IPA|fr|pjɛʁ fʁedeʁik saʁy}}; 10 March 1798, [[Saint-Affrique]] – 20 November 1861) was a French [[mathematician]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Accademia delle Scienze |url=https://www.accademiadellescienze.it/accademia/soci/pierre-frederic-sarrus |access-date=2024-05-03 |website=www.accademiadellescienze.it |language=en}}</ref>

Sarrus was a professor at the [[University of Strasbourg]], France (1826–1856) and a member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in Paris (1842).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sarrus |first=Pierre Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n5e56V-WFBUC&pg=PA1 |title=Recherches sur le calcul des variations: pièce pour le concours sur la question relative aux maxima et minima des intégrales multiples |date=1848 |publisher=Impr. Nationale |language=fr}}</ref> He is the author of several treatises, including one on the solution of numeric equations with multiple unknowns (1842); one on multiple [[integrals]] and their integrability conditions; and one on the determination of the orbits of the [[comets]].

Sarrus discovered a [[mnemonic]] rule for solving the [[determinant]] of a 3-by-3 [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]], named [[rule of Sarrus]]. He also demonstrated the fundamental [[Lemma (mathematics)|lemma]]{{Which|date=December 2025}} of the [[calculus of variations]]. Additionally, he also developed the [[Sarrus linkage]], the first linkage capable of transforming rotary motion into perfect straight-line motion, and vice versa. [[Sarrus numbers]] ([[Fermat pseudoprime#Definition|Fermat pseudoprime]]s to base 2) are also named after Sarrus, who discovered the first number (341).
